content: 1. Information Management in HIV Testing: Information management involves the use of both paper-based and electronic systems to record, store, and retrieve data. This includes records, documents, raw data, emails, and text messages that may provide testing results or reminders to clients. It is closely tied to documentation and record-keeping. All personnel involved in testing must work to minimize transcription errors. Assigning unique patient identification numbers at the health system level, and specimen identification numbers for each sample from the same individual, reduces the risk of errors and mix-ups. Linking a series of HIV test results is essential for retesting to confirm HIV-positive diagnoses and for clients with inconclusive results. Automated electronic readers for rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are becoming more available and can assist in data collection for program management and procurement planning. 2. Documentation and Record-Keeping: Documents include policies, processes, and procedural records for all aspects of testing services and quality management systems. These documents must be approved before use, revised as needed, reviewed annually, and removed when obsolete. Job aids guide test providers step-by-step through procedures, result interpretation, and assigning HIV status based on testing strategies. National programs should help testing sites develop site-specific standard operating procedures (SOPs) and job aids to improve the quality of HIV status reporting. Records generated from testing activities, including quality control (QC) and external quality assessment (EQA) results, maintenance logs, stock inventory, and corrective actions, must be accurately completed and securely stored for up to five years. These records must be readily accessible for retesting, referrals, and community-based testing services. 3. Occurrence Management: Occurrence management refers to processes for identifying and documenting non-conformances and implementing corrective actions. A non-conformance is any deviation from expected processes, such as missing or improperly followed procedures. Systems should be in place to monitor and detect quality issues or product problems, identify root causes, and implement corrective and preventive actions. Indicators such as turnaround times, rates of discrepant or invalid results, specimen rejection rates, and stock-outs should be routinely monitored to identify non-conformances. 4. Assessment of Testing Services: Internal assessments, often in the form of audits, should be conducted by supervisors or district health teams at least annually, preferably every three to six months. External quality assessments (EQA), such as proficiency testing, provide confidence in the accuracy and reproducibility of test results. Retesting is recommended for all individuals newly diagnosed as HIV-positive before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). 5. Process Improvement: Testing services must identify areas for improvement, plan and implement changes, and evaluate their effectiveness. Improvements can be made at the site, district, or national level, depending on the issue. Data from audits, EQA participation, and on-site supervision can guide corrective and preventive actions. Corrective actions address existing problems by eliminating root causes, while preventive actions aim to avoid potential issues. 6. Client Service and Satisfaction:g., healthcare workers) and external clients (e.g., individuals undergoing testing). Meeting client expectations involves delivering accurate results promptly and providing services in a non-discriminatory and non-stigmatizing manner. Privacy and confidentiality are critical. Feedback mechanisms, such as exit interviews and suggestion boxes, can help improve services. 7. Facilities and Safety: Testing facilities must be clean, comfortable, and well-maintained, with adequate lighting and climate control. Proper waste disposal for biological, chemical, and paper waste, as well as sharps, is essential. Confidentiality must be protected, including the use of separate waiting areas for additional testing. Staff should be trained in biological and chemical safety, and one staff member should act as a safety focal point at each site. 8. Quality Improvement in HIV Testing: Quality assurance is an ongoing process that requires continuous monitoring and evaluation of testing programs. Stakeholders at all levels must collaborate to maintain a functioning quality management system. Various quality improvement methods have been applied in healthcare, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, to address specific challenges in HIV testing services. This content outlines the critical components of quality assurance, client satisfaction, and safety in HIV testing services, emphasizing the importance of accurate documentation, continuous improvement, and adherence to best practices.
